outcomes: Compute raw preference scores from user and item embeddings
Train matrix factors with a stable regularized pairwise ranking loss
Keep held-out positives out of optimization
Calculate Recall@k, Precision@k, and nDCG@k from ranked candidates

embedding.name: embedding
embedding.definition: A vector representation of an entity or input, obtained from a lookup table or computed by an encoder.
embedding.explanation: This chapter learns lookup tables: a user or item ID selects one row, and training changes that row's coordinates. Other systems compute an embedding from an input with an encoder, such as a network that maps an image or text sequence to a vector. In this recommender, user and item embeddings share a latent space and their dot product is a raw preference score. Coordinates usually lack a unique human meaning because rotating every vector together can preserve all dot products. New users and items need a separate cold-start strategy.

matrix-factorization.name: matrix factorization
matrix-factorization.definition: An approximation of a user-item score matrix by products of lower-dimensional vectors.
matrix-factorization.explanation: If U holds user embeddings and V holds item embeddings, the predicted score matrix is approximately UVᵀ. Each score is one user-vector/item-vector dot product. The factor dimension controls capacity and computation. Factorization shares evidence through nearby vectors, which is useful when the observed interaction matrix is sparse. Missing entries are not automatically negatives; the objective must state how observed positives, explicit negatives, confidence, and unobserved pairs are treated.

pairwise-ranking.name: pairwise ranking
pairwise-ranking.definition: Learning to score a preferred item above a less-preferred item for the same user.
pairwise-ranking.explanation: A pairwise example contains a user, a positive item, and a negative item. Its margin is positive score minus negative score. The stable logistic loss softplus(−margin) becomes small when the ordering is correct and confident. Updating the user and both item vectors changes their relative position. Pairwise training aligns directly with ordering, but sampled or labeled negatives define the task and can introduce bias.

recall-at-k.name: Recall@k
recall-at-k.definition: For each query q with nonempty relevant set Rq, Recall@k is |Rq ∩ TopK(q)| / |Rq|, averaged across queries.
recall-at-k.explanation: Compute the fraction separately for each query, then average those query-level values so queries with many relevant items do not silently receive more weight. In this chapter each user is a query and has exactly one held-out relevant item, so Recall@k is one when that item appears in the top k and zero otherwise. Under this one-relevant-item condition Recall@k equals HitRate@k. With several relevant items, hit rate only asks whether at least one was retrieved, while recall counts how much of the complete relevant set was retrieved.

ndcg.name: nDCG
ndcg.definition: Normalized discounted cumulative gain, a ranking score that rewards relevant items near the top.
ndcg.explanation: DCG adds relevance divided by a logarithmic discount based on rank, so early relevant items contribute more. Dividing by the ideal DCG produces nDCG, usually between zero and one for nonnegative relevance. With one binary relevant item, the score is 1/log₂(rank+1), using one-based rank, when the item is within k. nDCG supports graded relevance, but its meaning still depends on which candidates and judgments were included in evaluation.

checks: Pairwise analytic and numerical gradients agree
Stable softplus remains finite at extreme margins
Training lowers the mean regularized loss over eight training triples
Ranking metrics average four query-level values over a declared candidate set that excludes training positives
limitations: The interaction matrix contains four users and six items with explicit course-authored negatives
Evaluation has one held-out relevant item per query, so its Recall@k is also HitRate@k
The model has two factors and no user/item biases
Cold start, exposure bias, diversity, fairness, and online impact are outside the executable
